response.response:
{
  "research_question": "How does mouse navigation performance vary across five stimulation paradigms (Combined, ICMS Only, Dim Visual Only, Bright Visual Only, and Sham) when measured by Time-to-Target, Success, Path Efficiency, Average Speed, and Angular Dispersion (AD)?",
  "stim_paradigms_compared": ["Combined", "ICMS Only", "Dim Visual Only", "Bright Visual Only", "Sham"],
  "response_variables": ["Time-to-Target", "Success", "Path Efficiency", "Average Speed", "AD"],
  "descriptive_findings": [
    "Success rates varied drastically, with the Sham group showing significantly lower performance (mean=0.273) compared to all stimulation groups (ranging from 0.673 to 0.785).",
    "Time-to-Target was longest in the Sham group (mean=4.68) and shortest in the Combined group (mean=2.56), indicating that stimulation generally reduces navigation latency.",
    "Path Efficiency was highest in the Bright Visual Only group (mean=0.504) and lowest in the Sham group (mean=0.308), suggesting that visual deprivation impair the ability to take direct paths.",
    "Average Speed was highest in the Combined group (mean=12.83) and lowest in the Sham group (mean=10.74), though differences between stimulation groups were smaller than those for success and efficiency.",
    "Angular Dispersion (AD), representing movement variability, showed a moderate range across groups, with the Combined group having the highest mean AD (0.399) and the Sham group the lowest (0.236), though the spread was narrower than for other metrics."
  ],
  "strongest_group_differences": [
    "The Sham group exhibits the most pronounced deficits across all metrics, particularly in Success (delta ~0.51 vs Combined) and Path Efficiency (delta ~0.195 vs Combined).",
    "The Combined group outperforms the Sham group in Time-to-Target by approximately 3.2 seconds and in Success by 50 percentage points.",
    "Among the stimulation-only groups, Bright Visual Only generally shows superior performance in Path Efficiency compared to Dim Visual Only and ICMS Only, though Success rates are comparable."
  ],
  "practical_interpretation": "Stimulation paradigms significantly enhance mouse navigation capabilities compared to the Sham condition, with the most robust improvements observed in task success and path efficiency. The 'Combined' paradigm appears to offer the best overall navigation speed and efficiency, while the 'Sham' condition results in poor performance characterized by low success rates, inefficient paths, and slow navigation. Visual-only stimulation (especially bright) supports better path efficiency than ICMS or dim visual stimulation alone.",
  "limitations": [
    "The analysis relies solely on mean statistics; variance and distribution shapes (e.g., skewness suggested by min=0, max=201.39 for Time-to-Target) are not examined.",
    "Mouse IDs are not aggregated by subject, so inter-subject variability and potential confounding effects of specific mice (e.g., SC21LM having the highest count) cannot be controlled or assessed.",
    "No inferential statistics (e.g., ANOVA, t-tests, confidence intervals) were performed to determine if observed mean differences are statistically significant.",
    "The sample size is heavily imbalanced, with the 'Combined' group comprising 64% of the total data (48,846 rows), which may influence the robustness of pooled summaries."
  ],
  "recommended_next_analysis": "Perform ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis tests for each response variable to establish statistical significance of group differences, followed by post-hoc pairwise comparisons with correction for multiple testing. Additionally, analyze the data by subject (Mouse ID) to account for inter-animal variability and potential outliers."
}
